18 Test principles

To display the Cell Blank Measurement Report, choose
Report > Setting. The report lists the current cell blank
values. The current cell blank values are compared to the
real-time cell blank values that are measured before every
measurement. The real-time cell blank values are
displayed on the Reaction Monitor Report.
The real-time cell blank value is defined as the mean value
of 3 cell blank measurements performed before every
sample measurement: (C1 + C2 + C3)/3.
If the difference between the real-time cell blank values
and the current cell blank value is greater than 0.1
absorbance units (Abs), an alarm is issued.

For endpoint assays based on an RCM or linear calibration,
the value under S1 Abs. equals the absorbance value of
calibrator 1 (Ab). For rate assays, S1 Abs. is the rate of
change in absorbance of the reaction with calibrator 1 (vb).
S1 Abs. is subtracted from the reaction absorbance of all
other patient samples, calibrators and QC materials.
The K-factor, as well as S1 Abs., is used in the result
calculation of every measured test.

On the Working Information dialog box, K-factors are

Application correction factor

Each calculated concentration result of a sample/control
can be corrected by the application correction factor and
offset. The application correction factor is assay-specific
and can be defined by Roche in the application setting.
The application correction factor allows either a
percentage correction or an additive correction (offset) of
the concentration result. Furthermore, a combination of
both corrections is possible.
For example, CREJ2 serum/plasma application. Due to the
non-specific protein reaction in the CREJ2 reaction, an
additive correction of -26 µmol/L will be carried out
automatically via an application correction offset. In
addition to this concept, the instrument factor and offset
are free for customer use.

About endpoint assays
There are 2 types of endpoint assays, the 1 Point assays
and the 2 Point End assays. These assay types show
different characteristics.

About 1 Point assays
A 1 Point assay is an endpoint assay without sample blank
measurement. It can be programmed for one or more
reagents. 1 Point means that the result calculation is
based on a single measuring point.
Further assay characteristics are the following:
•

(c 503) Any of the recorded measuring points 1 to 34
can be used a mp1.

•

(c 703) Any of the recorded measuring points 1 to 38
can be used as mp1.

Roche Diagnostics
cobas® pro integrated solutions · Software version 03-03 · User Guide · Publication version 4.2

Test principles

The absorbance reading can be taken during any disk
rotation after addition of the final reagent.

•

The reaction times for the selected application are
within the interval of 3–10 minutes.

•

The detectable reaction volume is 75–185 µL.

•

The mixable reaction volume is 60–185 µL.

A 1 Point assay can have reagents dispensed either at
R1 timing or at R1 and R2/R3 timing. The graphs can show
an increase or decrease in absorbance as the reaction
occurs.

About 2 Point End assays
A 2 Point End assay is an endpoint assay with sample blank
measurement. It can be programmed for two or more
reagents. 2 Point End means that the result calculation is
based on 2 measuring points. The first measuring point is
the sample blank reading, the second measuring point is
the final absorbance reading (endpoint).

18 Test principles

Further assay characteristics are the following:

2 Point End assay calculation

•

(c 503) Any of the 34 recorded measuring points can
be used as mp1 and mp2.

•

(c 703) Any of the 38 recorded measuring points can
be used as mp1 and mp2.

•

The first absorbance reading can be taken during any
disk rotation. Usually it is taken before or shortly after
the final reagent R2/R3 is added.

•

The second absorbance reading can be taken during
any disk rotation after the final reagent R2/R3 is
added.

•

The reaction times for the selected application are
within the interval from 3 to 10 minutes.

•

The detectable reaction volume is 75–185 µL.

•

The mixable reaction volume is 60–185 µL.

For a 2 Point End assay using reagents dispensed at
R1 and R2/R3 timing, the following variables are used in
the graph and the calculation:

About rate assays
There are 2 types of rate assays: Rate assays without
sample blank correction, and rate assays with sample
blank correction. The assay types show different
characteristics.

In this section

18 Test principles

About rate assays (1212)

About rate assays
Rate assays without sample blank correction can be
programmed for one or more reagents.
Further assay characteristics are the following:
•

(c 503) The allowed values for the measuring points
are: 1 ≤ mp1 < mp2 ≤ 34; mp1 + 2 < mp2

•

(c 703) The allowed values for the measuring points
are: 1 ≤ mp1 < mp2 ≤ 38; mp1 + 2 < mp2

Roche Diagnostics
cobas® pro integrated solutions · Software version 03-03 · User Guide · Publication version 4.2

Test principles

•

Rate of change in absorbance is calculated by least
squares method.

•

The reaction is monitored for linearity and substrate
depletion.

•

The reaction times for the selected application are
within the interval from 3 to 10 minutes.

•

The detectable reaction volume is 75–185 µL.

•

The mixable reaction volume is 60–185 µL.

1213

A rate assay is programmed for multiple measuring points.
There is a measuring window and every photometric
measurement within this window is considered for the rate
calculation. This means beginning with the reading at the
first programmed measuring point (mp1) through to the
reading at the second programmed measuring point (mp2).
The absorbance values are converted into the rate of
change in absorbance (vx) by least squares analysis. There
is no need for a dilution factor because all readings are
taken after the addition of the last reagent.

Absorbance

A rate assay can have reagents dispensed either at
R1 timing or at R1 and R2/R3 timing.

About high dose hook effect checks
The high dose hook effect check (or prozone check) is
used to detect a high dose effect of turbidimetric
immunology tests, which can lead to false low
concentration results. The high dose hook effect occurs
only with immunology tests measured on CC analytical
units with the photometric test principles.
The high dose hook effect check is performed with antigen
readdition method.

Roche Diagnostics
cobas® pro integrated solutions · Software version 03-03 · User Guide · Publication version 4.2

Test principles

1217

About the antigen readdition method
To check the high dose hook effect with the antigen
readdition method, additional reagent is added after the
sample measurement is completed.
For each calibrator set point, a rate of the specific
reaction (measuring window of the test) as well as the
antigen excess rate of the antigen readdition is
calculated. The system makes its calculation from two
curves, the calibration curve from the test reaction and
the curve from the antigen excess reaction. From this
antigen excess curve, a decision curve is generated using
the defined factor and offset. The decision curve is
reagent lot specific and is updated by full calibration
events. If the signal of the antigen excess rate of a sample
is below the decision curve, then the concentration result
of the sample is flagged.
If an alarm is issued, then an automatic rerun with
decreased sample volume is initiated.
This method of high dose hook effect is reagent lot
specific and cannot be combined with an autocalibration
or with copy-calibration.

About the kinetic unstable check
The kinetic unstable check can be used for the following:
•

Identification of atypical reaction kinetics revealing
test-specific problems

•

High dose hook effect detection with or without
antigen readdition

•

Detection of samples with an atypical signal above or
below a defined signal level

•

Detection of samples with an atypical signal between
or outside a defined signal range

The following can be defined for the Kinetic Unstable
Check:
•

Absorbance differences (defined by 2 measuring
points)

•

The absorbance of single measuring point

•

Calculation of the absorbance differences

•

Acceptance ranges for the calculated result

•

Rules for consequences (for example, rerun, data
alarm)

The kinetic unstable check can be applied to all test
modes.

Photometric measurements can be inaccurate under
certain conditions, for example impurities in the water bath
or precipitation during reaction. This affects the reaction
kinetics which can be seen in the reaction curve.
The kinetic roughness check (KR) is based on the variability
of the slope differences between 2 neighboring measuring
point sets over the reaction. Firstly, the slope between the
points is calculate. In a second step the slope is measured
point for point this time not taking the point as the basis of
the signal but the slope. The Kinetic Roughness Check is
test-specific and the parameters are defined in the
application settings.

1220

About sample index principles

About sample index principles
A number of diseases result in increased amounts of
chromogens such as bilirubin or hemoglobin, or lipemic
particles, which increase the turbidity of the sample.
These chromogens interfere with many photometric tests
and electrolytes. However, this interference can be
quantified by sample index measurements.
Sample indices are calculations of absorbance
measurements that provide a semi-quantitative
representation of levels of icterus, hemolysis, or lipemia
(turbidity) present in samples.
The system uses a separate, dedicated application using a
sodium chloride solution to determine the sample indices.

In this section
Definition of sample indices (1220)
Measurement of sample indices (1221)
Evaluation of sample indices (1222)
About sample index data alarms (1223)

Definition of sample indices

18 Test principles

Icterus index I

The icterus index, I, is reported in icterus units that are
linear, up to 60 mg/dL, and semi-quantitative. For
example, an icterus index of 20 is equivalent to a known
bilirubin concentration of approximately 20 mg/dL.

Hemolysis index H

The hemolysis index, H, is reported in hemolysis units that
are linear, up to 1000 mg/dL, and semi-quantitative. For
example, a hemolysis index of 500 is equivalent to a known
hemoglobin concentration of approximately 500 mg/dL.

Lipemia index L

The lipemia index, L, is reported in lipemia units
corresponding to Intralipid® (Kabi Pharmacia, Inc.), an
artificial lipid material. These units are linear, up to 2000,
and semi-quantitative. Hence, the L index provides an
estimate of the sample’s turbidity, not its concentration of
triglycerides.

Wavelength [nm]

If a test has a limit value other than 0, the sample index
check is activated for this test. In order to perform a
sample index check for a test, the sample index
measurement has to be ordered and performed
accordingly with each run. For the sample index
measurement, the system takes an aliquot of the sample,
dilutes it with 0.9% NaCl, and then measures the
absorbance values at 3 pairs of wavelengths:
•

For measurement of lipemia (L), wavelengths
700/660 nm are used because this range is free from
influence by hemolysis and icterus.

•

Hemolysis (H) is measured at 600/570 nm and
correction is made for absorption due to lipemia.

•

Icterus (I) is measured at 505/480 nm and correction
is made for absorption due to lipemia and hemolysis.

C, A, and D are sample dilution-dependent and unitdependent scale factors to provide semi-quantitative
interference levels. B, E, and F are correcting factors

independent of sample dilution since they are based on
ratios of absorbance values.

Overview of immunology principles - e 801

Overview of immunology principles - e 801
Three test principles are available for immunologic tests.
The competitive principle is used for small analytes, the
sandwich principle is used for larger analytes. The bridging
principle is used to detect antibodies in the sample.

ECL assay principles

Sandwich principle for high molecular weight analysis

Bridging principle to determine lgG and lgM

Competitive principle for low molecular weight haptens

Test principles

1225

About the competitive principle
This principle is applied to analytes of low molecular
weight, such as FT3.
•

In the first step, sample and a specific anti-T3
antibody labeled with a ruthenium complex are
combined in a cup.

•

After the first incubation, biotinylated T3 and
streptavidin-coated paramagnetic microbeads are
added. The still free binding sites of the labeled
antibody become occupied with formation of an
antibody-hapten complex. The entire complex is
bound to the microbead via interaction of biotin and
streptavidin.

•

After the second incubation, the reaction mixture
containing the immune complexes is transported into
the measuring cell. The immune complexes are
magnetically entrapped on the working electrode, but
unbound reagent and sample are washed away by
ProCell II M solution.

•

In the ECL reaction, the conjugate is a rutheniumbased derivative and the chemiluminescent reaction is
electrically stimulated to produce light. The amount of
light produced is indirectly proportional to the amount
of antigen in the sample.

18 Test principles

Evaluation and calculation of the antigen concentrations
are carried out by means of a calibration curve that was
established using calibrators of known antigen
concentration.

About the sandwich principle
The sandwich principle is applied to higher molecular
weight analytes, such as thyroid-stimulating hormone
(TSH).

Roche Diagnostics
cobas® pro integrated solutions · Software version 03-03 · User Guide · Publication version 4.2

Test principles

•

In the first step, the sample is combined with a reagent
containing biotinylated TSH antibody and a rutheniumlabeled TSH-specific antibody in a cup. During a 9minute incubation step, antibodies capture the TSH
present in the sample.

•

In the second step, streptavidin-coated paramagnetic
microbeads are added. During a second 9-minute
incubation, the biotinylated antibody attaches to the
streptavidin-coated surface of the microbeads.

•

After the second incubation, the reaction mixture
containing the immune complexes is transported into
the measuring cell. The immune complexes are
magnetically entrapped on the working electrode, but
unbound reagent and sample are washed away by
ProCell.

•

In the ECL reaction, the conjugate is a rutheniumbased derivative and the chemiluminescent reaction is
electrically stimulated to produce light. The amount of
light produced is directly proportional to the amount
of TSH in the sample.

About the bridging principle
The bridging principle is similar to the sandwich principle,
except that the assay is designed to detect antibodies, not
antigens (e.g., IgG, IgM, and IgA). This is accomplished by

Roche Diagnostics
cobas® pro integrated solutions · Software version 03-03 · User Guide · Publication version 4.2

Test principles

1229

including biotinylated and ruthenium-labeled antigens in
the reagents for which the targeted antibody has an
affinity.
•

In the first step, serum antibodies bind with the
biotinylated and ruthenium-labeled antigens to form
an immune complex.

•

The immune complex then reacts with streptavidincoated microbeads via the biotinylated antigen.

•

After the second incubation, the reaction mixture
containing the immune complexes is transported into
the measuring cell. The immune complexes are
magnetically entrapped on the working electrode, but
unbound reagent and sample are washed away by
ProCell.

•

In the ECL reaction, the conjugate is a rutheniumbased derivative and the chemiluminescent reaction is
electrically stimulated to produce light. The amount of
light produced is directly proportional to the amount
of analyte in the sample.

18 Test principles

Evaluation and calculation of the antibody concentrations
are carried out by means of a calibration curve that was
established using calibrators of known antibody
concentrations.

1231

About limit of detection and limit of
quantitation
It is important to fully characterize the analytical
performance of clinical laboratory tests in order to
understand their capability and limitations.

Relative frequency

The limit of detection (LoD) and limit of quantitation (LoQ)
describe the smallest concentration of a measurand that
can be reliably measured by an analytical procedure. The
LoD is the point at which analysis is just feasible. The LoQ
is the lowest concentration at which the analyte can be
quantitatively determined within predefined goals for bias
and imprecision.
Total error

Limits

Typically, LoQ will be found at a higher concentration than
LoD, but how much higher depends on the specifications
for bias and imprecision used to define it.
The LoD and the LoQ can be detected either by measuring
replicate samples with a low analyte concentration or by
an empirical approach, consisting of measuring
progressively more dilute concentrations of analyte.

1235

About calibration of ISE tests
The purpose of calibration is the assignment of a
concentration to a signal. For each calibration of ISE tests,
the calibrators are aspirated into the dilution vessel and
then transported through electrodes. After equilibration
occurs at the electrode, the electromotive force (EMF,
voltage) is measured.
The slope of the electrode is calculated based on the EMF
measurements and the set points of the calibrators.
An ISE calibration requires ISE Standard Low as calibrator
1 and ISE Standard High as calibrator 2 and 3. Refer to the
ISE Method Sheet for detailed information about the
calibrators to be used for an ISE calibration. An ISE
calibration is required every 24 hours and, for example,
after reagent exchange and electrode replacement.
Additionally, the concentration of the IS is determined
during the ISE calibration.
The AutoCal for ISE does not require any calibrator
material. For more details please refer to About AutoCal
for ISE (549).

In this section

concentration (1236)

About calibration of photometric tests

About calibration of photometric tests
The term calibration refers to the determination of a valid
relation between the measured value and the actual
concentration of the analyte. For endpoint assays, the
measured value is the absorbance, for rate assays, it is the
rate of change in absorbance. The graphical
representation of such relation is the calibration curve
also referred to as working curve.

Curve Type field: calibration curve types

•

•

Weighting: field: weighting mode for RCM Curve
Types (0, 1, 2, (3)). Weighting to assure more accurate
concentration values at calibrator set points with
lower absorbance

•

RCM Weighting field: in case of weighting mode (3)
input of individual weight factors for each calibrator
set point are necessary - not for curve type RCM2

•

Calibration method

The calibration that is performed on the system is an
update of the calibration curve. An update means that the
calibration curve is fitted to the new calibration results.
There are 3 methods to update a calibration:
•

1-point (re)calibration

•

2-point (re)calibration

•

Full calibration

u About calibration methods (1258)
u About calibration update types (1260)
Weighting

The weighting functionality favors those calibrator set
points with a lower absorbance or a lower rate of change
in absorbance. This enables a more accurate curve fit in
certain concentration ranges.
u About weighting (1261)

Lot and reagent pack calibration

When you load a new reagent lot on the system, a lot
calibration or a reagent pack calibration is performed.
Which calibration is performed depends on how long the
reagent pack is loaded on the system.
You can find more information about when and how a lot
and reagent pack calibration is used in the User Guide.

About calibration curve types
The calibration curve types describe the behavior of a
calibration curve and its mathematical function.

Overview of calibration curve types
The system uses different mathematical models to
describe the relation between the measured absorbance
and the concentration of the analyte of interest.

Linear calibrations

Linear calibrations are used for tests whose absorbance
values at different concentrations form a straight line. If a
linear calibration is based on 2 calibrator measurements, it
is termed linear 2-point calibration. If it is based on more

Roche Diagnostics
cobas® pro integrated solutions · Software version 03-03 · User Guide · Publication version 4.2

Calibration principles

1243

than 2 calibrators, it is termed linear multi-point
calibration. If all defined calibrator set points are used for
calibration, a linear calibration is termed as full calibration
and is not dependant on the number of calibrator set
points.

Calibration type

Nonlinear calibrations

Nonlinear calibrations are used for tests whose
absorbance values at different concentrations form a
nonlinear but reproducible plot. The non-linear calibration
functions RCM1, RCM2 and RCM5 can be fitted with 4, 5 or
6 calibrators. As the functions RCM3 and RCM4 have 5
parameters, the fit requires 5 or 6 calibrators.

Spline and line calibrations

In addition, there are 2 calibration types whose calibration
curves are piecewise defined interpolation functions:
spline and line graph.

About linear calibration
In general there are 2 procedures available; linear 2-point
or linear multi-point calibration and linear slope. For the
first case there are two parameters necessary, slope and
intercept. In certain cases the slope is given by the
application setting. For this situation only one calibrator is
necessary to calculate the corresponding intercept.

Absorbance

Absorbance

19 Calibration principles

Water is commonly used as calibrator 1. For linear 2-point
calibration, the absorbance of water and a second
calibrator is measured. These 2 points are used to
establish a linear plot, and its slope is used in the
calculation of subsequent QC and patient results.

Linear 2-point calculation

Slope

1245

The math model for a linear 2-point calibration is the
equation for a straight line y = a + b × x, where a is the yintercept and b is the slope. The equation’s variables are
defined as follows:
x=C

Concentration of the analyte

y=A

Absorbance (or rate of change in absorbance
for rate assays)

a

Absorbance when the concentration of the
analyte is 0

b

Ratio of the change in absorbance to the
change in concentration

The slope of a straight line can be derived either by the
formula b = (∆y)/(∆x) for 2 points or by the least squares
method for multiple points. For the first case, comparison
with the linear 2‑point calibration graph Cb ≠ 0 shows
∆y = AS2 – Ab and ∆x = Cs2 – Cb. The formula for the slope
can then be solved to b = (AS2 – Ab)/(CS2 – Cb). This equation
shows that b is equal to the reciprocal K‑factor. Therefore,
b = 1/K.
Where CS2 is the concentration value for calibrator 2.
Comparison with the linear 2-point calibration graph Cb ≠ 0
shows the y‑intercept a = Ab – (b × Cb), where Ab is the
absorbance and Cb the concentration value for
calibrator 1. With slope and y‑intercept determined, it is
possible to solve the equation y = a + b × x to x to calculate
the analyte concentration in a sample Cx:
z 1

y = a+bx

1
x = --  y – a 
b

x = Cx

y = Ax

By substitution of a, b, x, and y the following equation is
obtained:
z 2

Cx = K   Ax –  Ab – b  Cb  

Which is equivalent to Cx = [K × (Ax – Ab) + Cb]
2 additional constants are applied to this formula to
correct the result for systematic bias deriving from the
system. The calculation of the sample concentration is
shown in the following equation:

K-factor

A K-factor is used in the calculation of test results. Any
test requiring more than just calibrator 1 during calibration
has its K-factor calculated via the measured absorbances
of the calibrator 1 and the other calibrators

K-factor calculation

K-factors are calculated from absorbance and
concentration values for tests that are based on linear 2point or linear multi-point calibration curves.

19 Calibration principles

After a successful calibration, an updated calibrator 1
value (column) is displayed on the Working Information
dialog box on Calibration > Results. On the Calibration
Reaction Monitor Report, an updated value can also be
found. The absorbance value (or rate of change in
absorbance) of the second calibrator is found on
Calibration > Results. These new values are used to
calculate the K-factor, displayed on the Working
Information dialog box.

Endpoint assay example

The formula for endpoint assays is:
z 4

K =  CN – Cb    AN – Ab 

Cb

Concentration value for calibrator 1

CN

Concentration value for the second
calibrator (N), N > 1

Ab

Absorbance of calibrator 1 (S1 Abs.)

AN

Absorbance of the second calibrator (N), N > 1

Calibration principles

1247

A glucose test is calibrated with water as calibrator 1 and
a second calibrator with a concentration of 10.8. The
mean of the measured absorbance values is 0.0036 for
calibrator 1 and 0.8739 for the second calibrator.
The K-factor is calculated as follows:
z 5

K =  10,8 – 0,00    0,8739 – 0,0036 

K = 10,8  0,8703 = 12,41

This K-factor can now be used to calculate results from
test absorbance values.

The formula for rate assays is:

Cb

Concentration value for calibrator 1

CN

Concentration value for the second
calibrator (N), N > 1

vb

Rate of change in absorbance of the
reaction with calibrator 1

vN

Rate of change in absorbance of the
reaction with the calibrator (N), N > 1

An AST (aspartate aminotransferase) test is calibrated
with water as calibrator 1 and a second calibrator with a
concentration of 94.2 U/L. The mean of the measured
rates of change in absorbance is vb = –0,0006 for
calibrator 1 and vN = –0,0486 for the second calibrator.
The K-factor is calculated as follows:
z 7
Linear slope

K =  94,2 – 0,0    – 0,0486 –  – 0,0006  
K = 94,2   – 0,0480  = – 1962,5

Linear slope stands for a 1-point calibration using
calibrator 1 to calculate the intercept of the linear
calibration curve.

About spline calibration

Absorbance

When this calibration type is applied, the ranges between
the data points of the measured calibrators are
approximated by third degree polynomials. A smooth
calibration curve is thus obtained.

In the math model of a spline calibration, data points of
calibrators are taken as supporting points for the
determination of interpolating functions. The simplest
interpolating functions are used in linear interpolation,
where adjacent data points are connected by a straight
line. This method is used for line graph calibrations.
In contrast to the angular polygon of a line graph
calibration, a smooth curve results when using piecewise
polynomials of a higher degree for the interpolation. The
routine applied for spline calibrations determines a
smooth cubic spline approximation using third degree
polynomials.
Nonlinear spline calibration can be used with the following
assay types:
•

1 Point assay

•

2 Point End assay

•

Rate assay

About calibration methods
A calibration needs to be updated regularly. On the
system, the suitable method to update a calibration under
specific circumstances is predefined.
The update of a calibration can be described either as an
adjustment of parameters of the calibration curve or as an
adjustment of the measured value (signal correction) to
compensate for changed conditions. Both of these
descriptions are mathematically equivalent.

19 Calibration principles

calibration method.

A new concept of the cobas® systems is Automatic lot

Calibration signals can be separated into a systemdependent part (e.g, SNmod) and a reagent lot-dependent

Difference

Absorbance

The absorbance difference to the previous calibration is
measured for the one defined calibrator only, for example
for 1 Point A and 1 Point B update types. This difference
is then added to each of the test’s calibrator absorbance
values. This moves the calibration curve up or down,
maintaining its original slope.

Concentration

Ratio

Absorbance

The test’s absorbance value is measured with the one
defined calibrator only, for example for 1 Point A and 1
Point B update types. The ratio of this value to the
previous yields an adjustment factor. Each of the test’s
calibrator absorbance values is then multiplied by this
factor. This adjusts the slope of the calibration curve,
maintaining its original y-intercept.
Concentration

For a 2 Point update type, the options above are
combined. The calibration update occurs as described,
slope and y-intercept are adjusted.

It is possible to apply a weighting function during the curve
fitting process. The weighting function favors those
calibration points with a lower absorbance (or rate of
change in absorbance). This may result in a more accurate
curve fit in that particular concentration range.

Calculation without weighting

If weighting is not used (entry of 0 in the Weighting: field
on Menu > Application > Calibration), the curve fit is
optimized by varying the parameters of the calibration
function to minimize the sum of the residuals. The
residuals are the squares of the differences between the
actual absorbance values for each calibrator and the
absorbance calculated from the calibration function.

Weighting factor

The weighting factor is inversely related to the

be weighted differently. Explicit weighting is not usable for
curve type RCM2.

Calibration quality criteria

1263

y Calibration quality criteria and associated data alarms

SD limit

When calibrating nonlinear or multi-point linear tests, the
system performs the following test:
For each calibrator, an absorbance value is calculated
from the given concentration and the current calibration
curve. With these absorbance values, a calibration curve is
established. For each calibrator set point, the differences
between the calculated calibration curve value and the
measured absorbance value is determined. The residual
squares for each calibrator set point are summarized and
result in the SD value for the calibration curve fit. If the
determined SD value exceeds the SD limit, an SD.E alarm is
issued indicating a failed calibration. The calibration curve
of the affected test is not updated. The SD limit value is
defined in the SD Limit: field (in Abs.). An SD limit value of
0 denotes that the test is omitted.

Duplicate limit

All photometric calibrations are performed in duplicate.
The duplicate limit check calculates the % error (DE%) and
the absolute absorbance error (DEAbs.) (difference)
between these duplicate measurements.
If both the % error and the absorbance error are out of
range, a Dup.E data alarm is issued indicating a failed
calibration. The calibration curve of the affected test is
not updated.
u About the duplicate limit check (Dup.E) (1281)

Sensitivity limit

Sensitivity here refers to the ratio of an absorbance
difference to a concentration difference. It is calculated
from the measured absorbance values and given
concentration values of
calibrator set point M (SM = Sensitivity Start) and calibrator
set point N (SN = Sensitivity End):

About the calibration concept
Calibration procedure

A leading calibration curve is generated at Roche
Diagnostics during production of the reagent. At the
customer site, the system generates an update of the
leading calibration curve by measuring 2 calibrators under
routine laboratory conditions.

Calibration concept

A reference standardization curve utilizing master test kit
reagents and certified reference calibrator, for example,
World Health Organization (WHO) calibrator, is measured
at Roche Diagnostics. This curve uses 10–12 measuring
points (n = 10–12). The reference calibrator curve is the
basis for the production of leading calibrators.

four-parameter Rodbard function. The data characterizing

calibration is performed depends on how long the reagent
pack is loaded on the system.

About calibration quality criteria for immunology tests
Calibration quality criteria automatically verify the
reliability of calibrations. If a criterion lies outside the
configured quality limits, an alarm is issued.
For quantitative and qualitative tests, the following
calibration quality criteria are available:

Missing values

Duplicate measurements of 2 calibrators are used to
adjust the leading calibration curve stored on the reagent
container file.

19 Calibration principles

For quantitative assays 2, 4, or 5 calibrators can be used if
applicable.
If no value is missing, the calibration succeeds. If one value
is missing, the calibration fails.

Duplicate limit (Dup.E)

System error

To calculate the mean value of the duplicate
measurements of a calibration, the signal values are used.
The duplicate limit checks the signal values of each
replicate of a calibrator. If the difference between the
duplicate measurements is too great, the calibration fails.

If a hardware error occurs during a calibrator
measurement, the calibration fails.

Roche Diagnostics
cobas® pro integrated solutions · Software version 03-03 · User Guide · Publication version 4.2

Calibration principles

Minimum difference (Diff.E)

The minimum difference is defined as the difference in
percent between the values of calibrator 1 and 2. Limits
are given with the lot-specific container parameter of the
assay.

Calibration factor (Factor)

Each new lot calibration (L-Calib) uses a calibration factor
of 1. For all subsequent reagent pack calibrations (RCalib), a new calibration factor is calculated. The
calibration factor is the quotient of the slopes of the
currently performed calibration and the last valid lot
calibration for this reagent pack.
The limits are specified for each lot in the reagent
container file. If the calibration factor is outside the limits
(usually 0.8–1.2), the calibration is considered as failed.

1269

calibration factor criterion is only used for
i The
validating reagent pack calibrations.

Min/max signal

The measured signal of the calibrator should fall between
the designated minimum and maximum signal. Minimum
and maximum signals are test-dependent and are stored in
the reagent container file.
If any of the calibrator replicates fall out of the specified
min/max signal range, the calibration fails.

To calculate the limits of calibration quality criteria,
different factors should be considered.
Qualitative tests are calibrated by a scaling factor, the
cutoff value. The actual cutoff value is calculated using
the cutoff formula based on at least one reactive or nonreactive calibrator. Each sample receives a scaled result
value, the cutoff value, which allows for the classification
of samples being reactive or non-reactive.
For some tests in a range around a cutoff index = 1, no
determination regarding reactive or non-reactive results
can be made. This range is called the border area or gray
zone.

In order to calculate the result of a qualitative test (cutoff

measurement Seff with the cutoff signal of the calibration

Cutoff value of the calibrator

If the effective signal of the measurement Seff equals the

CutoffIndex equals 1. For effective signals being lower or
higher than the cutoff signal, the cutoff index is smaller or
larger than 1, respectively.
The test result is evaluated depending on the test
principle (sandwich or competitive):

Sandwich assays

Samples with a cutoff index ≥ 1.0 are considered reactive;
those with a cutoff index < 1.0 are considered nonreactive. For some tests, a gray zone is introduced.
result message is displayed in Calibration >

For qualitative sandwich tests, if the actual cutoff

index displayed after rounding is 1.00. The result
message Reac (reactive) is displayed.
If the actual cutoff index is 0.9995–0.9999 before
rounding, the cutoff index displayed is still 1.00
after rounding. However in this case the result
message NonReac (non reactive) is displayed.

1277

About data alarm rules for photometric
tests
The system checks several calibration quality criteria to
ensure that final results are valid. Data alarms appear on
the result report to indicate possible data errors and are
sent to the host. Some of the data alarms also trigger a
system alarm along with an audible signal. You can view
system alarms by choosing the Alarms button.

About the high dose hook effect check (Hook)
Some homogeneous immunology tests use the principle of
antigen/antibody complex formation (agglutination or
precipitation) as a measurement technique. The system
can measure turbidity caused by this specific agglutination
or precipitation by photometric means.
The antigen/antibody complex formation is predictable as
long as an excess of reagent (antibody) exists. However, in
samples with high levels of antigen, the reaction may begin
to reverse (deagglutination) because of the effect of the
excess antigen. This effect is called high dose hook effect
(or prozone effect).
If this phenomenon is not verified, abnormally high levels
of antigen in samples may give incorrect results.
The high dose hook effect check is applied as antigen
readdition method to any type of assay.

Antigen readdition

2 measuring points are defined in the Point1: and Point2:

Ranges

Linearity Limit

20 Rules for attaching data alarms

The system may check the high dose hook effect by
adding antigen as an additional reagent (R2 or R3). If the
reaction continues in the same direction (increasing or
decreasing absorbance) as the initial reaction, an excess
of reagent (antibody) still exists. This means that no high
dose hook effect occurs. If the reaction proceeds in the
opposite direction after additional antigen has been
added, the high dose hook effect is occurring, and the
result is invalid. The corresponding Hook data alarm is
attached to the result.

The Factor: field and the Offset: field define the antigen
decision curve.
For each calibration set point a rate of the specific
reaction (measuring window of the assay) as well as the
antigen excess rate (measuring points 1 and 2 of the
antigen readdition) is calculated. The system calculates
from that the calibration curve for the specific reaction of
the assay and secondly an antigen excess curve. From this
antigen excess curve a decision curve is generated using
the defined factor and offset. If the signal of the antigen
excess rate of a sample is below the decision curve, the
concentration result of the sample is flagged.

About the linearity limit check (>Lin)
To check the linearity of a rate reaction (rate of change in
absorbance), the percentage of nonlinearity is calculated.

The first 2 Linearity Limit fields indicate the linearity
limits (in Abs) for 4–8 measuring points and for 9 or more
measuring points (second field).
The Min. Total Rate: field and the Min. Diff. Rate: field
define additional conditions for the linearity limit check.
The Min. Total Rate: field defines a minimum rate of
change in absorbance (in Abs) for vx. If the measured rate
falls below this minimum, the linearity limit check is
neglected. This means, the Min. Total Rate: field defines
the variable T for the following condition:
If |vx| < T (in Abs), the linearity limit check is not performed.
The Min. Diff. Rate: field defines a minimum difference
between vi and vf (in Abs).

Roche Diagnostics
cobas® pro integrated solutions · Software version 03-03 · User Guide · Publication version 4.2

Rules for attaching data alarms

1281

If the measured difference |vf – vi| falls below this minimum,
the linearity limit check is neglected. This means, the Min.
Total Rate: field defines the variable D for the following
condition:
If |vf – vi| < D (in Abs), the linearity limit check is not
performed.

RCM Weight 1

A duplicate limit for calibrator acceptability is defined in
the application. To view this, choose Menu >
Application. In the AU drop-down list, choose the
analytical unit and then choose Calibration from the
second drop-down list. The entry in the first Duplicate
Limit: field defines the error limit in percent. The entry in
the second field defines the error limit in absorbance units.
For the duplicate limit check, the system calculates the
% error (DE%) and the absolute absorbance error (DEAbs.)
(difference) between these duplicate measurements. The
obtained values are compared to the values in the
Duplicate Limit: fields (% and Abs. field). If both the
% error and the absorbance error are out of range, a
Dup.E data alarm is issued indicating a failed calibration.
The corresponding values are calculated as follows:

will be checked against the sensitivity limit.

About the technical limit check (>Test/<Test)
The technical limit range is specified in the settings. To
view the technical limit range, choose Menu >
Application. In the AU drop-down list, choose the
analytical unit and then choose Analytical Parameters
from the second drop-down list. If a result does not fall
into the concentration range specified by the Technical
Limit: fields, the >Test or <Test data alarm is issued. The
>Test data alarm indicates results that exceed the upper
limit, <Test data alarm indicates results below the lower
limit.

to the currently chosen sample volume.

About the repeat limit check (>Rept/<Rept)
The repeat limit checks the final concentration (printed
concentration) of a test result. If the result is outside the
repeat limit but inside the technical limit, the test is
repeated using normal sample volume.

About the reaction limit check (>Reac0, >Reac1, >Reac2)
In rate or endpoint assays, correct data cannot be
obtained when the concentration or activity value is
beyond the quantitative range. For this reason, the
reaction limit is set to check if the measuring points are
outside this upper or lower absorbance limit.

w Reaction limits for descending (Decrease) and ascending (Increase) rate assays

For rate assays, data alarms are attached to the result
according to the following rules:
•

>Reac0: If no measuring point is within the reaction
limit.

•

>Reac1: If 1 measuring point is within the reaction
limit.

•

>Reac2: If 2-3 measuring points are within the reaction
limit.

For rate assays with ascending absorbance values, the
limit is an upper limit; for assays with descending
absorbance values, the limit is a lower limit. To view the
reaction limit value (absorbance limit), choose Menu >
Application. In the AU drop-down list, choose the
analytical unit and then choose the Ranges button. The
reaction limit value is displayed in the Abs. Limit: field.

Photometric
measurement range

Reaction limit

Endpoint assays

The value of the Reduction Point: field defines how many
measuring points must be within the reaction limit.
Example: Reduction Point: is set to 4 (minimum). This
means: If at least 4 measuring points are inside the
reaction limit, no data alarm is issued. All measuring points
inside the reaction limit are used for result calculation.
For result calculation, at least 2 measuring points are
necessary. If there is only 1 or 0 measuring point inside the
reaction limit, the first 2 measuring points are used for
result calculation.

To view the settings which define the measuring points to
be considered for the reaction limit check for endpoint
assays, choose Menu > Application. In the AU dropdown list, choose the analytical unit and then choose the
Ranges button.
•

Abs. Point1: field defines the first measuring point
(1 – 38).

•

Abs. Point2: field defines the last measuring point
(1 – 38).

20 Rules for attaching data alarms

The >Reac2 data alarm is attached to the result according
to the following rules:

Automatic correction of reaction limit
absorbance

•

Descending assays (Decrease): If the absorbance is
below the reaction limit.

•

Ascending assays (Increase): If the absorbance is
above the reaction limit.

The reaction limit is verified with reference to the
absorbance at the main wavelength. The system
automatically corrects the given reaction limit value, for
example, due to sample turbidity:
Reaction limit = absorbance limit + (LS – LC)
LS: The absorbance at a specific measuring point of the
primary wavelength during sample measurement. The
measuring point is defined in the Sample Blank Point:
field.
LC: The absorbance at sample blank point of the primary
wavelength during calibration using calibrator 1.
For increasing reactions the reaction limit has a maximum
value of 3.3 independent from the absorbance limit in the
application setting and independent from the difference
LS – LC.

Roche Diagnostics
cobas® pro integrated solutions · Software version 03-03 · User Guide · Publication version 4.2

Rules for attaching data alarms

1287

The reaction limit value is displayed in the Limit column on
Calibration > Results > Reaction Monitor. The value of
LS fluctuates for every sample measurement, which results
in a different reaction limit value.
If LS < LC, the reaction limit value is the same as the value in
the Abs. Limit: field defined in the settings. To view the
value, choose Menu > Application. In the AU drop-down
list, choose the analytical unit and then choose the
Ranges button.

Glossary
absorbance

barcode scan zone

Relation between the intensity of light at a specified
wavelength that has passed through a reaction mixture
and the intensity of the light before it enters the
reaction mixture.

Area of consumables and accessories in which a
barcode label needs to be placed in order to avoid
barcode read errors.

accuracy
Degree of conformity of a measured value to a
standard or a true value.

Basic Wash

that is used to clean parts of a system.

calibration

on the Serum Work Area instruments.

Process of checking if an instrument is working

calibration

Process of checking if an instrument is working
accurately by comparing known standards with
measurement results delivered by this instrument.

analyte

Constituent of a sample with a measurable property.

calibration curve

analytical unit

Plot of measured signal values (determined during
calibration) versus known concentration values of
calibrators.

Component of a system that consists of one or more
units in which the test is performed, the actual
measurement takes place, and the analytical result is
generated.

application code number
Test code that identifies an application on a system.

assay reagent
Reagent that is necessary to perform one or multiple
tests according to a specified test principle.

calibration factor

calibration and the last valid lot calibration for the
respective reagent pack.

calibration factor

stable within specified and documented limits.

calibration profile

conditioning

User-defined set of tests to be calibrated as a group.

Process of preparing parts of the instrument which are

calibration quality criterion
Set of reference values that is used by the instrument
software to automatically evaluate the validity and
reliability of the generated calibration.

calibrator
Measurement standard used in calibration.

carryover
Contamination of a sample by reagents or a sample of
a previous run or contamination of a reagent by a
previously pipetted reagent.

cerebrospinal fluid
Sample type that consists of selective ultrafiltrate of
the plasma surrounding the brain and the spinal cord.

check digit
Additional digit at the end of a barcode that is used to
verify correct barcode reading.

circuit breaker
Automatically or manually operated electrical switch
designed to protect an electrical circuit from damage
caused by overload or short circuit.

copy calibration
Feature that allows to copy calibration data from
primary ACN to the additional ACN of the same type
(on the same reagent pack).

copy calibration
Feature that allows to copy calibration data from
primary ACN to the additional ACN of the same type
(on the same reagent pack).

copy QC
Feature that allows to copy QC data from primary ACN
to additional ACN of the same type.

cup
Small container used for sample, calibrator, QC
material or reagent. Depending on the type of cup and
system it can be placed in a rack, on a tube or loaded
directly onto the system. Compared to a tube, it allows
the use of smaller liquid volumes and so reduces the
dead volume.

cup on tube
Configuration in which a cup is placed on a tube
instead of being placed directly in a rack.

cleaning wire

cutoff value

Wire that is used for removing blockages in probes or
reaction cell rinse nozzles.

For qualitative tests, value that indicates a clinically
significant amount or the presence of an analyte in the
sample. Below this value, a qualitative test result is
determined to be negative and above positive.

clinical chemistry
Medical discipline that is specialized in measuring and
analyzing body fluids for diagnostic and therapeutic
purposes.

clot detection
Feature used in the aspiration system that detects if a
pipette tip or a probe/needle is clogged with clot.

data alarm
Additional piece of information associated with a test,
QC or calibration result. It is caused by the abnormal
condition of measurement.

data alarm
Additional piece of information associated with a test,
QC or calibration result. It is caused by the abnormal
condition of measurement.

Volume of a liquid that is left in a container after

reasons.

Registered product name for an additive that reduces

degasser
Unit that removes air bubbles from the fluid system and
helps to improve both accuracy and precision in
systems where dissolved gases cause problems.

deproteinizer

components that come in contact with a sample.

deproteinizer
Liquid used during maintenance to deproteinize

detection unit
Unit in which measurement takes place and a signal is
transferred into an electronic signal.

dilution
Process of adding a material, usually a liquid or gas, to
another material or substance, resulting in a decrease
in concentration of the former.

electrochemiluminescence
Luminescence produced during electrochemical
reactions in solutions. It is used in immunological tests
as a highly sensitive and selective method. It combines
analytical advantages of chemiluminescent analysis
with ease of reaction control by applying electrode
potential.

electrochemiluminescence
Luminescence produced during electrochemical
reactions in solutions. It is used in immunological tests
as a highly sensitive and selective method. It combines
analytical advantages of chemiluminescent analysis
with ease of reaction control by applying electrode
potential.

emergency stop

Process of stopping the system as soon as possible in

dilution factor

expected values

Range of predefined values of test results expected for

drive line

expiration date

transport lines as well as for transporting sample

Upper limit of the time interval during which the

duplicate repeat test

filling volume
Volume of a liquid with which a container is filled.

Components through which different liquids flow
during operation or maintenance.

Components through which different liquids flow

Sample index that is reported in hemolysis units. It

host
External information system of higher level that

instrument alarm
Alarm caused by the abnormal condition of an

instrument factor
Fixed multiplier used to convert numeric results. It can
be used to convert units.

internal standard solution
Solution with stable properties that contains
predefined concentrations of Cl-, K+ and Na+ ions and
that is used to determine ion concentration values of
samples.

ion-selective electrode
Electrode that is used to measure the concentration of
an ion in a sample.

icterus index

Flow path of an ISE measuring unit.

Sample index that is reported in icterus units. It
provides an estimation of the bilirubin concentration.

ISE Internal Standard supply nozzle

immunoassay
Test type that uses an immunological reaction of
antibodies. It measures the formation of antibodyantigen complexes in blood samples or other body
fluids and it is used when an analyte needs to be
detected in a qualitative or quantitative manner.

immunochemistry
Branch of immunology that is concerned with the
chemical and biochemical detection of immune
reactions.

incubation bath
Temperature-controlled, incubation water-filled
reservoir that surrounds the reaction cells.

Nozzle that dispenses ISE Internal Standard into the
dilution vessel in the ISE unit.

ISE reference electrode
Electrode that is used to close the measurement
circuit on ISE measuring units.

ISE sipper nozzle
Sipper nozzle that aspirates the reaction mixture from
the dilution vessel into measuring block.

laboratory automation
Automatically controlled operation of a laboratory that
is performed by mechanical, electronical, or IT devices.

limit of quantitation

lot number

Lowest amount of analyte in a sample that can be
accurately quantitated with a certain total allowable

Unique identification of a lot.

lipemia

Smallest concentration of analyte that can be reliably
measured by an analytical test.

Elevated number of fats or lipids in a sample.

liquid level detection
Process during which the fill level of a liquid in a
container is determined.

liquid waste
Liquid that remains after the system operation. It
contains sample, reagents, and system reagents. As it
is potentially biohazardous it has to be disposed
according to local regulations.

LLD
Process during which the amount of liquid in a

Component by which samples in racks are loaded onto

lot
Definite amount of some product, material, or service
collected together and submitted for examination or
consumption.

lot calibration
Calibration that is done for one reagent pack/reagent
cassette loaded onto the instrument for less than 24
hours and valid for all reagent packs/reagent cassettes
from the same lot.

lower limit of measurement
Smallest concentration of analyte that can be reliably

main line
Transport line that transports racks from the sample

maintenance action
Action that needs to be carried out to keep laboratory
instruments in good condition. It can either refer to a
single action or to a procedure consisting of several
steps.

maintenance interval
Interval between maintenance actions.

maintenance pipe
Set of software-controlled maintenance actions
arranged in a batch set. It can be used to have certain
maintenance actions occur automatically in a defined
sequence without any user interaction required.

masking
Process of temporarily preventing the system from
performing certain activities or accessing a selected
item.

measurement precision
Closeness of agreement between measurement
indications or measured quantity values obtained by
replicate measurements on the same or similar objects
under specified conditions.

measurement unit
Definite quantity, defined, and adopted by convention,
that is used as a standard for measurement.
